title: In 76,215 human genomes, 437,000 predicted conserved RNA structures in non-coding DNA show no detectable pairing-specific constraint: paired and unpaired conserved bases are equally depleted
abstract: In human genetic variation, the predicted base pairs of about 437,000 conserved RNA structures in non-coding DNA show no detectable sign that natural selection keeps them: at bases conserved in mammals, paired bases are no more depleted of variants than unpaired bases, and alleles that break a pair are not rarer than alleles that keep it. This matters because genome-wide screens for conserved RNA structures are used as evidence that much of the non-coding genome works as folded RNA. We counted gnomAD v4.1 alleles (76,215 genomes) at 24.4 million bases of 437,337 CRSs (structures predicted by CMfinder; Seemann et al. 2017), 1.3 million bases of 33,056 EvoFold structures, 313 tRNA genes and 396 miRNA precursors, at sites with the same base in human, chimpanzee and gorilla, against a 5-base context model from 15 million flanking bases. For alleles with frequency 1e-4 or more, CRS bases conserved in mammals (phyloP >= 2.27) were 18% depleted, and the ratio of observed/expected at paired to unpaired bases was 0.995 (95% CI 0.977 to 1.014); it was 0.953 (0.919 to 0.990) in EvoFold and 0.55 (0.37 to 0.86) in miRNA precursors. In a G-C pair the transition C->U keeps a pair (G-U wobble) while G->A and all transversions break it; in an A-U pair A->G keeps it. The pairing depletion, the fraction of pair-breaking alleles missing relative to pair-keeping alleles (against unpaired bases), was 47% (14 to 66) in tRNA stems, 0.9% (-1.7 to 3.8) in CRSs and -3.7% (-20 to 11) in EvoFold; without the unpaired baseline it was 36% (13 to 52) in tRNAs and 0.0% (-2.0 to 2.0) in CRSs. If selected pairs lose half of their pair-breaking alleles, at most 7.5% of CRS pairs can be under such selection; if selection is as weak as at conserved CRS bases, about 21%. With the pre-registered primary outcome (any allele), which was near saturation in tRNAs, CRSs on the transcribed strand of genes showed a small pairing depletion (2.2%, 0.9 to 3.5) absent on the other strand; its cause is unknown. A false signal at G-U pairs came from derived human reference bases; an ancestral filter removed most of it. Limits: the tRNA control rests mainly on one contrast, and the test sees only selection strong enough to change allele frequencies in humans.
